explain.title: What is the cell cycle?
explain.body: The textbook defines it as: “It is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.” The cell cycle has two main phases: interphase and the mitosis phase.

explain.title: Interphase: most of the cell cycle
explain.body: Interphase lasts for about 90% of the total time of the cell cycle. The cell performs its life functions and prepares for the next division. It consists of G1, S, and G2 phases.

explain.title: G1 and S phases
explain.body: G1 is also called the growth phase: the cell grows, makes proteins and organelles, and makes enzymes needed in S phase. In S phase, the DNA of each chromosome is copied. Each chromosome then consists of two sister chromatids, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.

explain.title: G2, M, and G0 phases
explain.body: In G2, the cell grows further, makes proteins for division, checks for DNA damage, and prepares for mitosis. After interphase, M phase divides the cell into two daughter cells. Some cells enter G0 and stop dividing while carrying out specialized functions; neurons may remain there indefinitely, while epithelial cells continue to divide.

mistakes: Do not say that the chromosome number doubles in S phase; the DNA is copied, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Do not confuse G1 and G2: G1 is the first growth phase, while G2 follows DNA replication and includes preparation for division.
Do not say that every cell enters G0; the textbook notes that some cells, such as epithelial cells, continue to divide without entering G0.
Do not describe interphase as a resting phase; the cell performs life functions, grows, copies DNA, and prepares for division.

explain.title: What mitosis does
explain.body: Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell. It occurs in the somatic cells of eukaryotes.

explain.title: The two major parts
explain.body: There are two major phases of mitosis i.e. karyokinesis and cytokinesis. Karyokinesis means the division of the nucleus. Cytokinesis is the division of cytoplasm.

explain.title: The four phases of karyokinesis
explain.body: In prophase, chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the nuclear envelope and nucleolus break down. In metaphase, chromosomes attach to spindle fibres and line up at the equator. In anaphase, sister chromatids separate and move towards the poles. In telophase, new nuclear envelopes form, the nucleolus reforms and chromosomes unfold back into chromatin.

explain.title: Cytokinesis in animal and plant cells
explain.body: In animal cells, a furrow develops at the equator and a ring of microfilaments contracts, pinching the cell into two. In plant cells, Golgi vesicles fuse in the middle to form a plate called phragmoplast; it grows outward and its membranes fuse with the cell membrane.

explain.title: Why mitosis matters and what can go wrong
explain.body: Mitosis supports growth, cell replacement, regeneration and asexual reproduction. If mitosis is not properly regulated, cells may divide uncontrollably and form tumours. Tumours that invade other tissues are malignant tumours (cancer); spreading of disease is called metastasis.

mistakes: Do not say mitosis halves the chromosome number: each daughter cell has the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
Do not mix up anaphase and metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator in metaphase, while sister chromatids separate in anaphase.
Do not confuse karyokinesis with cytokinesis: karyokinesis is division of the nucleus, while cytokinesis is division of the cytoplasm.
Do not describe plant cytokinesis as an inward-moving cleavage furrow; the book describes Golgi vesicles forming a plate that grows outward.
Do not call every tumour cancer: a tumour that stays in its original location is benign; a tumour that invades other tissues is malignant.

explain.title: What meiosis does
explain.body: It is the type of cell division in which each daughter cell receives half the number of chromosomes as compared to the parent cell. In meiosis, a diploid parent cell divides to produce four haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: Diploid and haploid
explain.body: Diploid means the cells in which chromosomes are in pairs (homologous pairs) while haploid means the cells with half number of chromosomes i.e., cells with no pairs of chromosomes.

explain.title: The first division
explain.body: In meiosis-I, the homologous chromosomes in a diploid cell separate and so two haploid daughter cells are produced. In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair, form tetrads and can exchange portions by crossing over.

explain.title: The second division
explain.body: Meiosis-II closely resembles mitosis. Sister chromatids separate during anaphase-II, and the process ends with four haploid daughter cells.

explain.title: Why meiosis matters
explain.body: Meiosis helps maintain chromosome number across generations and contributes to genetic diversity. Non-disjunction can make gametes with more or fewer chromosomes than normal.

mistakes: Do not say sister chromatids separate in anaphase-I; homologous chromosomes separate then, while sister chromatids separate in anaphase-II.
Do not confuse synapsis (pairing of homologous chromosomes) with crossing over (exchange of chromosome portions).
Do not say meiosis produces two daughter cells in total; meiosis-I produces two cells, and meiosis-II results in four.
Do not call the daughter cells diploid; they have half the parent cell’s chromosome number and are haploid.
When describing genetic diversity, explain that crossing over creates new gene combinations.

example.question: Compare mitosis and meiosis in terms of number of divisions, daughter cells, chromosome number, and crossing-over.
example.answer: Mitosis has one division and produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent; it does not involve crossing-over. Meiosis has two divisions and produces four daughter cells with half the chromosome number; crossing-over occurs and variations are produced.

explain.title: What the two divisions share
explain.body: DNA replication occurs during interphase (S phase) before both divisions. Both divisions also involve chromosome condensation, spindle formation, and the stages prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase. Cytokinesis occurs at the end of both divisions.

explain.title: How many cells are made
explain.body: In mitosis, a parent cell divides once and produces two daughter cells. In meiosis, a parent cell undergoes two divisions and produces four daughter cells.

explain.title: How chromosome number changes
explain.body: In mitosis, the chromosome number in daughter cells remains the same as the parent cell. In meiosis, the chromosome number is reduced by half in daughter cells.

explain.title: Pairing and crossing-over
explain.body: In mitosis, homologous chromosomes do not form pairs and crossing-over does not occur. In meiosis, homologous chromosomes form pairs and crossing-over occurs during prophase. This helps produce variations.

explain.title: Where and why they occur
explain.body: Mitosis occurs in somatic cells and supports growth, development, and maintenance. Meiosis occurs in germ line cells and produces gametes in animals and spores in plants for sexual reproduction.

explain.title: When sister chromatids separate
explain.body: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase in mitosis. In meiosis, they separate during anaphase II; homologous chromosomes separate during anaphase I.

mistakes: Do not say meiosis produces two daughter cells; it produces four.
Do not say the chromosome number stays the same in meiosis; it is reduced by half.
Do not confuse homologous chromosomes separating in anaphase I with sister chromatids separating in anaphase II.
Do not say crossing-over occurs in mitosis; it occurs in prophase of meiosis.
When describing metaphase, distinguish a single chromosome aligning in mitosis from homologous pairs aligning in meiosis.

explain.title: Interphase prepares the cell
explain.body: Interphase includes G1, S and G2. The cell grows and carries out its activities in G1, replicates DNA in S, and prepares for division in G2.

explain.title: Mitosis makes matching cells
explain.body: Mitosis is nuclear division in somatic cells. Prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase lead to two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent.

explain.title: Cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm
explain.body: Animal cells form a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two. Plant cells form a cell plate that develops into a new cell wall.

explain.title: Meiosis reduces chromosome number
explain.body: Meiosis has two divisions. Homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis-I, reducing chromosome number; sister chromatids separate in meiosis-II.

explain.title: Meiosis creates variation
explain.body: Crossing over in prophase-I and independent assortment create new genetic combinations. Meiosis produces haploid cells and helps maintain a species' chromosome number after fertilization.

notes.title: The Cell Cycle: Growth, DNA Copying and Division
notes.answer: The cell cycle is the series of events that take place in a eukaryotic cell from its formation to its division into two daughter cells.
notes.explanation: The cell cycle is an ordered series of events in which a eukaryotic cell grows, copies its DNA, and divides into two daughter cells. Interphase includes G1, S, and G2. In G0, some cells stop dividing to carry out special functions.
notes.simple: A cell grows, copies its DNA, prepares, and then divides. Some cells pause dividing in G0.
examples: In S phase, the DNA is copied, but the total number of chromosomes remains the same.
Neurons can remain in G0 for an indefinite period, while epithelial cells continue to divide.
steps: After M phase, the cell enters G1 and grows.
In S phase, the cell copies its DNA.
In G2 phase, the cell grows further and prepares for division.
In M phase, the cell divides into two daughter cells.
Some cells may leave the cycle and enter G0.
notes.checkQuestion: In which phase is the DNA of each chromosome replicated?
notes.checkAnswer: S phase; the DNA is replicated, and the total number of chromosomes remains the same.

notes.title: Mitosis: making two matching cells
notes.answer: Mitosis is the type of cell division in which a cell divides into two daughter cells, each with the same number of chromosomes as were present in the parent cell.
notes.explanation: Mitosis makes two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. It has two major parts: karyokinesis, the division of the nucleus, and cytokinesis, the division of the cytoplasm.
notes.simple: Mitosis is like copying a cell: the copied chromosomes are shared between two new cells, so each new cell has the same chromosome number as the original.
examples: When skin cells are replaced, mitosis makes new cells that are exact copies of older cells.
In Hydra, mitosis helps a bud grow into a new individual.
steps: First, the nucleus divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Then, cytokinesis divides the cytoplasm.
The result is two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell.
notes.checkQuestion: During which phase of mitosis do sister chromatids separate?

notes.title: Meiosis: making haploid cells
notes.answer: Meiosis produces four haploid daughter cells from one diploid parent cell.
notes.explanation: Meiosis makes four haploid cells from one diploid parent cell. In meiosis-I, homologous chromosomes separate; in meiosis-II, sister chromatids separate. For example, crossing over exchanges portions of non-sister chromatids, while non-disjunction can give gametes too many or too few chromosomes.
notes.simple: Meiosis is a two-division process that makes four cells, each with half the parent cell’s chromosome number.
examples: Crossing over can produce new combinations of genes.
If chromosomes fail to separate properly, non-disjunction may produce gametes with an abnormal number of chromosomes.
steps: In prophase-I, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over can occur.
In anaphase-I, homologous chromosomes separate into two haploid sets.
In meiosis-II, sister chromatids separate.
At the end, four haploid daughter cells are formed.

notes.title: Comparing Mitosis and Meiosis
notes.answer: Mitosis produces two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. Meiosis produces four daughter cells with half the chromosome number.
notes.explanation: Mitosis has one division and makes two daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent. Meiosis has two divisions and makes four daughter cells with half the parent cell’s chromosome number. Crossing-over occurs in meiosis and helps produce variation.
notes.simple: Mitosis makes two similar cells. Meiosis makes four cells with half the chromosome number, and crossing-over can make them varied.
examples: If a parent cell has 8 chromosomes, mitosis produces daughter cells with 8 chromosomes each.
If a parent cell has 8 chromosomes, meiosis produces daughter cells with 4 chromosomes each.
steps: Check how many divisions take place: one in mitosis and two in meiosis.
Compare the number of daughter cells: two in mitosis and four in meiosis.
Compare chromosome numbers: unchanged in mitosis and reduced by half in meiosis.
Look for crossing-over: it occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.
Remember that sister chromatids separate in mitosis and in anaphase II of meiosis.
notes.checkQuestion: How many divisions occur in meiosis, and when do sister chromatids separate?
notes.checkAnswer: Meiosis has two divisions; it separates sister chromatids during anaphase II.

notes.title: The cell cycle and cell division
notes.answer: Mitosis produces two genetically identical daughter cells with the same chromosome number as the parent cell. Meiosis produces cells with half the chromosome number and contributes to genetic variation.
notes.explanation: The cell cycle is the sequence of events in which a cell grows, copies its DNA and divides. Mitosis makes two genetically identical cells with the same chromosome number; meiosis makes cells with half the chromosome number and creates genetic variation.
notes.simple: A cell first grows and copies its DNA. Then it divides. Mitosis makes two matching cells; meiosis makes cells with half the chromosomes.
examples: In the S phase, DNA is copied so each chromosome has two sister chromatids.
In mitosis, sister chromatids separate during anaphase. In meiosis, homologous chromosomes separate in meiosis-I and sister chromatids separate in meiosis-II.
steps: Interphase: the cell grows during G1, copies DNA during S, and prepares for division during G2.
Mitosis: the nucleus divides through prophase, metaphase, anaphase and telophase.
Cytokinesis: the cytoplasm divides to form two daughter cells.
Meiosis: two nuclear divisions produce cells with half the original chromosome number; crossing over helps create variation.
notes.checkQuestion: When do sister chromatids separate in mitosis?
notes.checkAnswer: Sister chromatids separate during anaphase of mitosis; in meiosis they separate during anaphase-II.
